standard_prerequisites.name: Descent of the property of being a closed immersion for algebraic spaces along an fpqc covering
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Descent on Spaces, Lemma labelled spaces-descent-lemma-descending-property-closed-immersion (canonical Stacks tag 0420); invoked at proof lines 1978-1979
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies that X -> X' is a closed immersion once its base changes are; the surjectivity step and the assembly into a thickening are retained in the counted span.

core_obligations: Unwind the statement for algebraic spaces: for a morphism X -> X' of algebraic spaces over a scheme S and an fpqc covering {g_i : X'_i -> X'} whose base changes X_i -> X'_i are thickenings, show X -> X' is a thickening (proof lines 1972-1975).
Get surjectivity: since the g_i are jointly surjective, X -> X' is surjective (proof lines 1976-1977).

Conclude: descent of the closed-immersion property for algebraic spaces along the fpqc covering makes X -> X' a closed immersion, hence a thickening; the author leaves the first order case unproved (proof lines 1977-1982).
proof_roadmap: Translate fpqc locality into the concrete descent statement for a covering of the target algebraic space (proof lines 1972-1975).
Use joint surjectivity to get surjectivity of X -> X' (proof lines 1976-1977).
Apply descent of closed immersions for algebraic spaces and conclude, leaving the first order case to the reader (proof lines 1977-1982).
difficulty_reason: The lemma states that the property of being a thickening of algebraic spaces is fpqc local on the target, and likewise for first order thickenings (statement lines 1967-1968). The proof follows the same two-ingredient pattern as its scheme-level counterpart but has to use the descent statement for algebraic spaces: joint surjectivity of the covering gives surjectivity of X -> X', descent of the closed-immersion property over algebraic spaces makes X -> X' a closed immersion, and a surjective closed immersion is by definition a thickening (proof lines 1976-1980). The author explicitly leaves the first order case unproved, and that sentence is reproduced as written. The claim is H2: short, one reduction, no construction of its own.
